summary.text: The equivalence principle is the hypothesis that gravitational mass and inertial mass are numerically equal because of a fundamental identity in nature.
Its weak form says masses of any composition in free fall take the same trajectories and land at identical times.
Einstein's extended form, which also requires special relativity to hold in free fall, was a critical input for developing general relativity.

facts.label: Galileo's finding
facts.value: Gravitation is independent of the amount of mass accelerated

facts.label: Windowless room
facts.value: 1g of gravity and 1g of acceleration look the same

items.prompt: You wake in a windowless room and feel pressed to the floor with the force of 1g. What can you conclude about where you are?

options.label: You must be resting on a planet's surface
You must be in a spaceship at a standstill
You cannot tell a planet from a ship accelerating at 1g
You must be in free fall far from everything

items.explain: An observer cannot distinguish a uniform gravitational field of 1g from a spaceship accelerating at 1g, since the observations are indistinguishable.

items.prompt: Newton timed pendulums made of different materials and found identical periods. What did he infer?

options.label: Heavier materials fall faster in the end
Gravitational and inertial mass are the same thing
Materials do not matter, but length changes mass
Air resistance is the only force on a pendulum

items.explain: From identical periods he inferred that gravitational and inertial mass are the same thing, which later became known as weak equivalence.

items.prompt: In Newton's picture, objects of different mass falling together is an accident of nature. How does Einstein's picture treat it?

options.label: As an unexplained coincidence, just as Newton did
As a result of how masses are measured by a scale
As a feature that holds only for very light objects
As a consequence, because the same mass causes and answers to gravity

items.explain: In Einstein's model mass causes spacetime curvature and then moves through spacetime according to that curvature, so the equivalence follows from physics.

items.prompt: Two objects made of different materials are released at the same moment from the same spot, with no other forces acting. What does the weak principle predict?

options.label: They follow the same path and land together
The denser one lands first
The lighter one drifts off to the side
The softer one lands first

items.explain: Freely falling test particles follow the same trajectories once an initial position and velocity are prescribed, whatever they are made of.

items.prompt: Why must an experiment testing the Einstein form of the principle be small?

options.label: Large labs are too costly to build
Big setups are affected by variations in the field
Small setups give faster falls than big ones
Big setups cannot be made to fall freely

items.explain: The setup must be small compared to variations in the gravitational field (tidal forces) and small enough that its own gravity does not change the result.

items.prompt: A theorist wants a version of the principle that covers a planet or star held together by its own gravity. Which form is meant for that?

options.label: The weak form
The Einstein form
The Galilean form
The strong form

items.explain: The strong form allows freely falling bodies to be massive gravitating objects, including astronomical bodies with gravitational self-binding energy.

paragraphs.heading: Two masses, one thing
paragraphs.text: Careful experiments show that an object's inertial mass and its gravitational mass come out as the same number, whatever the object is made of. The equivalence principle is the hypothesis that this match is no coincidence. It says the two are equal because, at root, they are the same thing.

paragraphs.heading: The windowless room
paragraphs.text: A simple picture makes the idea concrete. Imagine you are shut in a room with no windows. You cannot tell whether you are sitting in a uniform gravitational field of 1g or riding in a spaceship in deep space that is speeding up at 1g, because everything you observe will look exactly the same. In this way the principle stretches the principle of relativity, which says the laws of physics stay the same under uniform motion.

paragraphs.heading: Galileo and Newton
paragraphs.text: The weak form of the principle has been known for centuries. By testing how different materials accelerate, Galileo Galilei found that gravity does not depend on the amount of mass being accelerated. Some 50 years later Isaac Newton asked whether gravitational and inertial mass might be different ideas. He compared the swing periods of pendulums made of different materials, found them identical, and concluded the two masses are the same. This version, in which bodies of any make-up fall along the same paths and land together, came to be called weak equivalence.

paragraphs.heading: Accident or consequence
paragraphs.text: One way to state the idea is to assume that a gravitational field and a matching acceleration of the frame of reference are fully equivalent in every physical way. That makes it impossible to speak of absolute acceleration, just as ordinary relativity rules out absolute velocity, and it makes the equal fall of all bodies seem natural. In Newton's law the principle is just an observed accident of nature, but in Einstein's model it is a consequence of physics. There, the same mass both causes gravity, by curving spacetime, and responds to it, by moving through that curvature.

paragraphs.heading: Putting it to the test
paragraphs.text: Highly precise experiments have squeezed any possible departure from equivalence down to very small amounts. Such tests must be local: the setup has to be small compared with changes in the gravitational field, called tidal forces, and small enough that its own gravity does not alter the result. With these limits alone, Einstein was able to predict the gravitational redshift. The weak and Einstein forms are checked with very different kinds of experiments.
